2122.tone: Binary/privative tone: H vs Ø, TBU = mora (long vowels and syllabic sonorants count). Lexical tone (noun and verb minimal pairs, p. 87) and grammatical tone (predication, relativisation, tense; pp. 87-88). Two spreading rules: High-Tone Doubling (one mora rightward, applies word-internally and across words, restricted at the right edge of a prosodic unit, where the doubled H on the penult mora is realised as falling) and long-distance spreading between two primary Hs. Toneless noun stems receive a predictable H on M2 of the word (§3.3.1.2). Downdrift and non-automatic downstep (§3.2). §3.6.3 treats extra-high pitch on certain moras as intonational 'rhetorical emphasis', not stress. The words 'stress' (outside 'mistress') and 'accent' (outside diacritic names and one bibliography title) do not occur; the grammar never posits stress or accent.

2125.exq_: His analysis, although by no means final, shows that the Citak phonemic system is richer than that of any of the other Asmat languages. The following outline is based on Bromley's reports.
2125.tone: Bromley's tentative inventory includes 3 tonemes, but the tonal contrast is 'restricted to monosyllabic words' (three pitch patterns: 1. short low or downglide; 2. short and high; 3. long upgliding high), clearer in the Tiau dialect than in Senggo; in Senggo part of the speakers have lost the 1 vs 2 contrast, keeping 1+2 vs 3 as syllable length, and others realise 1 vs 2 as syllable-onset character ('surging' vs 'sharp, ballistic' onset; fn. 35 Bromley p.c.). Voorhoeve adds that 'much of the system could be described as exhibiting stress contrasts'. Bi-/polysyllabic words have phonemic stress, not tone. tone or pitch accent is the defensible alternative label if the 3-toneme inventory is given priority; lexical chosen because the only word-stress statement is contrastive/phonemic stress with no default position.

2128.tone: No tone is posited for Classical Tibetan. Beyer 1992 addresses tone once, at p. 22 fn. 22 (ch. 2 'History'): 'we have not discussed the development of apparently phonemic tones in Lhasa City-both tone REGISTERS, with different tone heights developing from voiced and voiceless onsets in Old Tibetan, and tone CONTOURS, with different tonal shapes developing from syllable-final vowels, glides, and stops in Old Tibetan.... There is no reason to believe that Old Tibetan had tones; if Proto-Tibetan ever had phonemic tones, the system had disappeared long before historical times.' DeLancey 2003 (Classical Tibetan, in Thurgood & LaPolla eds., The Sino-Tibetan Languages, sec. 2 Phonology; in the copy consulted under narp1239) states 'There is no evidence for tonal distinctions in Classical Tibetan'. Hahn's Lesson 1 high/low tones and Hannah 1912's pitch/'emphasis' classes belong to the modern Lhasa reading pronunciation, not to the classical language.

2130.prule: Root-final stress: stress falls on the last syllable of (almost every stressed) root; affixal material on both sides is stressless — prefix syllables (ngu-bizh 'sol', p.41; adjectival n-/na-, p.56) and the dependent-pronoun suffixes/enclitics (-a, -(a)l, -i, -e, -xaꞌ... 'no tienen acento... actúan como sufijos', p.53), so in lizha 'mi casa' (lizh + -a) stress is on the root syllable, not the word-final one. In compounds the rightmost member's stressed syllable carries the primary stress (ntsiki, niliwen, p.43). Position therefore follows the root/affix division, not a syllable count of the word.
2130.srule: Only stated for compounds: the rightmost member's stressed syllable receives the main stress ('la sílaba acentuada que está más a la derecha es la que recibe el acento principal': ntsiki 'echar lumbre', niliwen 'sanar'), implying weaker stress on the stressed syllables of non-final members; no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned for non-compound words (Benton 2016, Apéndice I §§1-5 pp.41-44, Apéndice II §2.1.2 p.53 read).

2130.tone: Tonal language with stress described separately from tone. Apéndice I §4 (p.43): five tones — alto, medio, bajo, bajo ascendente, alto descendente — marked in the vocabulary but not in ordinary orthography; 'Los tonos de una palabra no son alterados por los tonos de palabras que la antecedan o la sigan', though the potential-aspect prefix and the 1sg dependent pronoun cause complex tone changes. §5 (pp.43-44): an additional 'sílaba fuerte' vs 'sílaba normal' syllable-type contrast (phonetically shorter vowel, higher tone, sometimes rapid intensity drop), 'aparte de los tonos', not written — a lexical contrast on the stressed syllable, not a stress-placement matter. Stress ('sílabas acentuadas') conditions allophony: o -> [u] in unstressed syllables (p.41), glottalized ('quebradas') vowels only in stressed syllables 'con todos los tonos' (p.42), fortis consonants long right after a stressed syllable (p.43); adjectives with n-/na- 'frecuentemente tienen un tono ascendente en la sílaba acentuada' (p.56). Juárez Santiago 2018 (pp.9-22) counts four tones.

tn.quote: En el zapoteco de Coatecas Altas se presentan los siguientes tonos: alto, medio, bajo, bajo ascendente, y alto descendente. Normalmente, en la forma escrita del zapoteco de Coatecas Altas no se indican los tonos, pero en el vocabulario están incluidos para indicar la pronunciación exacta, usando varios tipos de acentos. ... Los tonos de una palabra no son alterados por los tonos de palabras que la antecedan o la sigan. Sin embargo, el prefijo del aspecto potencial y el del pronombre dependiente de la primera persona del singular sí causan cambios complejos en los tonos de las palabras.
tn.translation: In Coatecas Altas Zapotec the following tones occur: high, mid, low, low rising, and high falling. Normally the tones are not indicated in the written form of Coatecas Altas Zapotec, but in the vocabulary they are included to show the exact pronunciation, using several kinds of accent marks. ... The tones of a word are not altered by the tones of words that precede or follow it. However, the potential-aspect prefix and that of the first person singular dependent pronoun do cause complex changes in the tones of words.

2132.prule: Accent position is lexically contrastive: most monomorphemic words (which are mostly disyllables) carry the accent on the penultimate syllable, but a small percentage are oxytone or proparoxytone, and the source demonstrates the contrast with four minimal pairs of disyllabic nouns (ˈkala 'straw' / kaˈla 'leg'; nugi 'poporo lime' / nuˈgi 'plague, crazy'; munʒi 'woman' / munˈʒi 'malanga'; mugi 'swollen' / muˈgi 'agouti'; the print marks only kala's penult, the other first members are unmarked and penult by implication). No predictive rule is given; penultimate is the statistical default.
2132.srule: Only in compounds: the phonological word has one main accent; in compound words of four or more syllables a secondary accent is perceived on the syllable that carried the accent of the component lexeme in its free form (the component not bearing the compound's main accent), e.g. {ˈuaka + huˈaba} -> /ˈuakahuˈaba/ 'mejilla'. No secondary or rhythmic stress is described for non-compound words (Ortíz Ricaurte 2000, §3.1.1.2 A, §3.1.3.1, read pp. 759-761, 766-768).

2133.prule: Primary stress falls, with few exceptions, on the last syllable of the ROOT (root-final), not of the word: merána'e 'is listening' (root mera-, ra = root-final; -na and -'e are suffixes). When suffixes are added the stress may move onto one of the suffixes (past -ca before declarative -'e: meracá'e 'listened', stress on the suffix ca) or, rarely, to another syllable of the root; the -chi 'of' example shows stress moving within the root, not onto the suffix (lápalo 'lizard' -> lapalóchi 'of the lizard': ló is the root-final syllable, -chi is unstressed). Stress is contrastive in a few pairs (dehuí 'brush' vs déhui 'a kind of fish'; mérana'e 'is waiting' vs merána'e 'is listening'); déhui, mérana'e and bare lápalo are not root-final, so the 'few exceptions' are exemplified but not characterised as a class. Higher pitch is the stated correlate of the stressed syllable.
2133.srule: Not mentioned in Moore 1975 [1972] (p. 5, the 'acento prosódico' paragraph, which is the article's whole treatment of stress; pp. 1-7 read): one stress per word is described and placed; no secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress is discussed. 2134.prule: Culminative word stress on the root/stem syllable: each word has exactly one stressed syllable, 'usually the last'. Major lexical classes are typically a single stressed syllable; the first syllable of complex stems, verbal prefixes and proclitics are unstressed pretonic syllables; the only posttonic material is reduced (enclitic) person-of-subject / possessor pronouns, which are unstressed. Pace 1990: 22 adds that 'the verb root never occurs unstressed'. Stressed syllables are further either ballistic or controlled (a syllable-type contrast, not a placement contrast).

tn.quote: 1.7. Tone. Because of the interplay of tone with stress and other elements of the syllable, it is convenient to speak of eight types of syllable: the class product of ballistic/controlled, long/short, and open/checked contrasts. With this clarification, the tones may be introduced. A stressed syllable may occur (1) with any of three simple tones: low /L/, mid /M/, or high /H/; or (2) with any of four tone sequences: two upglides (low-mid /LM/ or low-high /LH/) and two downglides (high-mid /HM/ or high-low /HL/).

tn.quote: Dans un environnement où les langues à tons prédominent, des tons apparaissent en swahili de Lubumbashi, bien que ce parler soit issu d'une langue non tonale (swahili). Cependant, le rôle de ces tons reste assez limité. Kapanga (1993) montre la fonction des tons dans l'extension verbale en aka. L'extension àkà à tons bas est utilisée avec le marqueur verbal na pour exprimer l'habituel, alors que cette extension avec des tons hauts (áká utilisée avec le futur et le passé) est utilisée pour exprimer un passé ou un futur lointain.
tn.translation: In an environment where tone languages predominate, tones appear in Lubumbashi Swahili, although this variety derives from a non-tonal language (Swahili). However, the role of these tones remains rather limited. Kapanga (1993) shows the function of tones in the verbal extension aka. The extension àkà with low tones is used with the verbal marker na to express the habitual, whereas this extension with high tones (áká, used with the future and the past) is used to express a remote past or future.

2142.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the phonological word; fixed, quantity-insensitive (syllables are (C)V, no weight contrast), non-contrastive. The phonological word = grammatical word plus any following monosyllabic enclitic postposition/particle, so a single enclitic carries the stress and, with stacked enclitics, the last one does.
2142.srule: Only in (diachronically) complex words -- historical compounds that are not synchronically segmentable: secondary stress on the last syllable of the first (historical) morpheme, whatever the number of following syllables (hinomadini [hiˌnu̜madi'ni] 'daughter-in-law', hidobadi [hiˌdo̜ba'di] 'son-in-law'). No rhythmic secondary stress is described; simple words are transcribed with one, final, stress.

2148.prule: No word stress. Dagbani is a tone language (two level tones, H and L, plus downstep; a possible falling tone in the Eastern dialect). The two reachable first-hand modern descriptions, both by native-speaker phonologists, deny stress outright: Inusah 2021 'Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking... stress does not exist in the phonology of the language' (reporting Hudu 2007's duration/intensity measurements, which found no phonetic correlate for the syllables Olawsky called stressed), and Hudu 2022 'In a non-stress language like Dagbani' / 'the more prominent syllable does not bear stress'. Hudu 2022 posits a left-headed bimoraic (trochaic) foot inside the prosodic word on segmental/phonotactic evidence only, explicitly not stress.
2148.srule: Not mentioned in Inusah 2021 (ch. 5 'Suprasegmental phonology', pp. 155-158 and 192; literature review p. 29) or Hudu 2022 (pp. 272-274; sec. 3.2 pp. 287-288): both deny word stress of any degree ('Dagbanli like other Mabia languages is not stress marking'; 'a non-stress language like Dagbani'), so no secondary or rhythmic stress arises; Hudu 2022's left-headed bimoraic trochaic foot is diagnosed by segmental criteria and its head syllable 'does not bear stress'.
